answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, proxy wording per binding condition):

In the NLSY79 extract, the Black–non-Black/non-Hispanic difference in BA-track attainment — operationalized as ever being recorded in a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence in 1981–1983, because no post-1979 education variable exists in the file — is NOT a Black advantage at any SES level. Instead, the racial gap in college-enrollment/BA-track attainment grows systematically more negative as SES rises: among low-SES families the gap is essentially zero (Black 2.8% vs 2.3% non-Black/non-Hispanic; +0.6 pp, p≈0.39), it is small and nonsignificant at mid SES (3.5% vs 5.0%; −1.5 pp, p≈0.15), and it becomes large and highly significant at high SES (6.8% vs 16.8%; −10.1 pp, p<0.0001). The race×SES interaction is significant (LRT = 12.14, 2 df, p = 0.0023; Black×High-SES OR = 0.29, p = 0.0006). Hypothesis: increments of family SES translate into far larger BA-track attainment gains for non-Black/non-Hispanic respondents than for Black respondents, so racial parity in BA-track attainment holds only at the bottom of the SES distribution and racial disparities are widest among the most advantaged families. Hispanic respondents do not show this pattern (High-SES rate 19.4%, near parity with non-Black/non-Hispanic 16.8%), indicating the SES-amplified gap is specific to the Black–non-Black/non-Hispanic contrast. All results must be read as college-enrollment/BA-track attainment, never literal BA degree completion.

KEY EVIDENCE:

1. Proxy strength (binding condition #3): residence code 3 (DORM/FRAT/SORORITY) recorded for 579 respondents in 1981, 498 in 1982, 516 in 1983; 1,017 respondents proxy-positive in ≥1 wave; 432 (42.5%) positive in more than one wave, supporting genuine college attendance rather than one-off coding. Construct check: proxy-positive respondents were no better educated by 1979 (12.3% with ≥13 grades vs 11.4%), which is expected because the 1979 grade variable predates the enrollment window for most respondents (aged 14–22 in 1979); this also illustrates why 1979 schooling cannot serve as the outcome.

2. Primary gap table (composite SES = tertiles of mean z-score of max parental education and log 1979 family income; complete cases n = 9,904 of 12,686 = 78.1% retained; logistic n = 7,502 Black+non-Black/non-Hispanic):
  Low SES: Black 2.8% (n=881) vs 2.3% (n=1419), gap +0.6 pp, p=0.39; Hispanic 3.8%
  Mid SES: Black 3.5% (n=401) vs 5.0% (n=1981), gap −1.5 pp, p=0.15; Hispanic 7.5%
  High SES: Black 6.8% (n=311) vs 16.8% (n=2509), gap −10.1 pp, p<0.0001; Hispanic 19.4%

3. Logistic regression (colEnroll ~ black × SES tertile + sex + age79): interaction LRT = 12.14, p = 0.0023; Black main effect OR = 1.13 (p=0.65) at Low SES; Black×Mid OR = 0.52 (p=0.10); Black×High OR = 0.29 (p=0.0006).

4. Sensitivities (all confirm the monotonic widening of the Black–non-Black gap with SES):
  - Income-only quartiles (1979 income): gaps +0.1 (Q1), −2.1 (Q2, p=0.011), −2.9 (Q3, p=0.037), −13.4 pp (Q4, p<0.0001); interaction LRT = 11.70, p = 0.0085.
  - Wealth-added SES (adds signed-log 1985 net wealth; NONRANDOM SUBSET, n = 7,934 = 62.5% of file): gaps −3.7 (Low, p=0.0005), −3.0 (Mid, p=0.015), −10.0 pp (High, p<0.0001) — same direction, larger low-SES deficit.
  - Winsorized top-1% income: identical to primary (+0.0/−1.7/−10.8 pp) — results not driven by income outliers.
  - Missing-SES indicator category (no listwise deletion): Missing-SES respondents show a −7.9 pp gap (Black 1.7% vs 9.6%), i.e., SES missingness is itself race-correlated; primary conclusions unchanged.

5. Negative wealth (711–1,248 rows per wave) retained as legitimate negative net worth via signed-log transform; income has no negative codes (min 0); top-coding at $75,001 in 1979 income noted. NLSY sentinel codes ≥90 in education set to missing.

PROXY LIMITATION (stated plainly, per binding condition #2): The dataset contains no education variable after 1979 — no later-wave highest-grade-completed, no degree field, no diploma indicator — so literal BA degree completion cannot be measured. The dorm/fraternity/sorority residence code in 1981–1983 was chosen as the only direct marker of college attendance in the file; multi-wave persistence (42.5% of proxy-positives) supports its validity, but it captures enrollment around ages ~16–26, not verified degree conferral.

ASSUMPTIONS/UNCERTAINTIES: (a) outcome is a residence-based enrollment proxy, not BA completion; (b) SES measured at/before 1979 (family of origin), while enrollment occurs 1981–1983; (c) complete-case SES drops 21.9% of rows nonrandomly (missing-SES category shows a −7.9 pp gap); (d) wealth-added variant uses a self-selected subset; (e) Hispanic cohort reported separately, not pooled; (f) the study-context note (nls_raw.domain_knowledge.1) was applied: explicit missing-data handling throughout, saving/spending, incarceration-via-residence, and test-score/class-rank variables were inspected but not needed for the core SES–race–attainment design.

SUBMISSION CONTRACT: answer = hypothesis above; payload.hypothesis = same; payload.workflow = executed workflow described below; artifacts.analysis = analysis.py (executed, nonempty, 183 lines) plus five CSV outputs in outputs/.

payload.hypothesis: In the NLSY79 extract, there is no Black advantage in college-enrollment/BA-track attainment (ever recorded in a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence in 1981–1983; no post-1979 education variable exists in the data, so literal BA completion cannot be measured) at any socioeconomic status level. The Black–non-Black/non-Hispanic gap is essentially zero among low-SES families (+0.6 pp, n.s.), small at mid SES (−1.5 pp, n.s.), and large at high SES (−10.1 pp, p<0.0001), with a significant race×SES interaction (LRT=12.14, p=0.0023; Black×High-SES OR=0.29). Hypothesis: each increment of family SES yields substantially larger BA-track attainment gains for non-Black/non-Hispanic respondents than for Black respondents, so racial parity in BA-track attainment exists only at the bottom of the SES distribution and racial disparities are widest among the most advantaged families; the pattern is specific to the Black–non-Black/non-Hispanic contrast (Hispanic respondents reach near-parity at high SES, 19.4% vs 16.8%).
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 rows × 61 columns). Cleaned NLSY sentinel codes (≥90) in education to missing; retained negative family net wealth as valid negative net worth (signed-log transform); income had no negative codes. Outcome: binary college-enrollment/BA-track proxy = residence code 3 (dorm/frat/sorority) in any of 1981–1983 (1,017 positive; 42.5% positive in >1 wave), explicitly a proxy because the file's only education variable is 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (respondents then aged 14–22). SES: composite index = mean of z(max of mother's/father's highest grade completed) and z(log 1979 total net family income), split into tertiles; strict complete cases retained (9,904/12,686 = 78.1%). Primary evidence: Black-vs-non-Black/non-Hispanic enrollment-rate gap within each SES tertile, and logistic regression colEnroll ~ black × SES-tertile + sex + age79 with LRT for the interaction; Hispanic cohort (n=2,402) reported separately throughout. Sensitivities: income-only quartiles; wealth-added composite (adds signed-log 1985 net wealth, flagged nonrandom subset n=7,934); winsorized top-1% income; missing-SES indicator category. All computations in analysis.py; tables exported to outputs/.
